title: GST_112 — End of Semester Objective Exam

questions.q: A study of a people records their chieftaincy titles, the rules governing who may marry whom, and the courts that settle their disputes. Which component of culture is being recorded?
questions.why: Chieftaincy, marriage rules and courts are institutions and norms, which is the sociological component. Ideological covers the beliefs and values a people hold. Technological is material culture, the tools, artefacts and buildings they make. Associational is one of the two forms of society, not a component of culture at all.

questions.q: A thinker proposes that farms, factories and mines should be owned in common and the wealth they produce shared out among all. Whose vision of society is this?
questions.why: Marx envisioned a communist society built on collective ownership of the means of production and the distribution of wealth, which is exactly common ownership plus sharing. Functionalism says nothing about ownership; it views society as an organism in which each component plays a crucial role. An associational society is a form of grouping marked by specialised labour and contractual ties. Nation-building is mobilising resources for development and constructing a national identity.

questions.q: Colonialism altered three domains of African society. Which of the following is NOT one of them?
questions.why: The three domains are governance, culture and family structures, with pre-colonial Yoruba communities as the worked example of reshaped households. Trade routes is the plausible outsider: colonial rule certainly redirected trade, but trade is not one of the three domains named for African societies.

questions.q: In a settlement, membership comes by birth into a lineage, work is shared with little specialisation, and tradition binds behaviour tightly. Which form of society is this?
questions.why: All three markers point one way: undifferentiated division of labour, kinship-based interaction and a strong hold of tradition make this a communal society. An associational society has the opposite profile on the same three bases, with specialised labour, impersonal or contractual interaction and weaker tradition. A communist society is Marx's ownership arrangement, and colonial society is not one of the two categories used here.

questions.q: A government mobilises resources for socio-economic and political development while running campaigns to construct a shared national identity. Which process is this?
questions.why: Nation-building has both halves, mobilising resources for socio-economic and political development and constructing a national identity, and both appear here. National integration is narrower: it is the welding of a diverse population into one community, the outcome rather than the whole process. Functionalism is a theory of how society works, and colonialism is foreign rule.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the methods used to study nation-building and national integration in Nigeria?
questions.why: The methods are historical analysis, document review, case studies, government policy evaluation, surveys and interviews, and comparative analysis. Laboratory experiment is the outsider: it belongs to the natural sciences, while the other three appear on the list word for word.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about culture and society is correct?
options: Culture is the people themselves organised as a group
Society is the system of traditional behaviours, beliefs, practices and values
Culture is what a people share; society is the people themselves organised as a group
Culture and society are interchangeable names for the same thing
questions.why: Culture is a complex system of traditional behaviours, beliefs, practices and values, that is, what a people share; society is the grouping of the people themselves, sorted into communal and associational forms. The first two options each take one definition and attach it to the wrong term. The fourth denies a distinction that the two definitions make plain.

questions.q: Which of the following best defines national integration?
options: Mobilising resources for development and constructing a national identity
The binding of a diverse population into a single national community
A complex system of traditional behaviours, beliefs, practices and values
Collective ownership of the means of production and distribution of wealth
questions.why: National integration is the binding of a diverse population into one national community, and it is presented as Nigeria's central challenge, with ethnic diversity as the main hurdle. The first option is nation-building, the process rather than the outcome. The third is the definition of culture. The fourth is Karl Marx's communist society.

questions.q: Nigeria has over 348 groups of one kind and over 374 of another. Which pairing is correct?
questions.concept: Nigeria's language and ethnic group figures
questions.why: There are over 348 language groups and over 374 ethnic groups, so the larger number is the ethnic one: more peoples than tongues. The second option is the classic swap. The third and fourth keep one figure right but invent a category, dialects or kingdoms, that is never counted.

questions.q: Benin's military expansion reached several peoples and towns before colonial rule. Which of the following was NOT among them?
questions.why: Benin's expansion reached Auchi, Idah, Itsekiri, Urhobo, Isoko and Okpe, with a military expedition as far as Eko, which is Lagos. Idoma belongs to the other conquest list: the Jukun extended influence over the Kanuri, Hausa, Igala, Idoma and Ebira. Jukun conquests ran north and middle belt, Benin's ran south and west.

questions.q: Two sub-groups say the gods they worship are still located in an Ijaw town, a legacy of wars that moved people about. Which town is it, and what does the case illustrate?
options: Patani, and cultural diffusion resulting from wars
Onitsha, and religious borrowing through trade
questions.why: The Emowa and Isoko sub-groups say their gods remain at Patani, an Ijaw town, and this is given as cultural diffusion occurring as a result of wars. Epe is where Kosoko fled after the 1851 bombardment, a different century and topic. Idah is one of the towns Benin's expansion reached. Onitsha is one of the Delta ports of 1857, and the point here is diffusion through war rather than through trade.

questions.q: The land of one people served as the trade corridor linking the hinterland Igbo with the coastal Efik and Ijaw. Which people?
questions.why: Ibibio land was the corridor between the hinterland Igbo and the coastal Efik and Ijaw. The Nupe traded shea butter, bangles, brasswork, potash and straw hats with the Yoruba, well to the north west of this route. The Itsekiri and Urhobo appear as peoples Benin's expansion reached, not as the corridor between hinterland and coast.

questions.q: A deity worshipped by the Yoruba is traced back to a Nupe original. Which pairing is correct?
options: Igunu, traced to the Nupe Ndakogbaya
Ibini Ukpabi, traced to the Ibibio
questions.why: The Yoruba Igunu is traceable to the Nupe Ndakogbaya, which is why it is offered as evidence of contact between the two peoples. Ibini Ukpabi really is of Ibibio origin, but it ended up with the Igbo, not the Yoruba. Ekpe originated among the Efik and spread to some Igbo subgroups. The Bori cult is common throughout Hausaland. Only the first pairing links Yoruba to Nupe.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the pre-colonial origin legends is correct?
options: Saif is the ancestor claimed by the Hausa
Bayajidda married the daughter of the Ooni of Ife
Kisra founded the Hausa and Kanuri kingdoms
The Bayajidda legend shows historical ties between the Gwari, Nupe and Yoruba
questions.concept: Traditions of origin as an indicator
questions.why: The Bayajidda legend is cited as evidence of ties between the Gwari, Nupe and Yoruba peoples. Saif is the Kanuri ancestor and Bayajidda the Hausa one, so the first option swaps them. Bayajidda settled among the Kanuri and married the Mai's daughter, not the Ooni's. Kisra founded the Yoruba and Borgu kingdoms and considered the Ooni of Ife his brother.

questions.q: The people of one geo-political zone once thrived under a democratic age-grade system. Which zone is this?
questions.why: The age-grade system is the democratic socio-political system of the Igbo of the South East. The South South, home to the Edo, Itsekiri, Ijaw and Efik, is credited with democratic systems and influential kingdoms but not with age grades. The North East is Kanuri and Jukun with unique socio-political systems, and the North Central is the most ethnically diverse zone.

questions.q: What does cultural diffusion mean?
options: The interaction between two or more distinct linguistic and cultural groups
The spread of cultural elements from one group to another
The grouping of a people into communal and associational forms
The exchange of goods between regions that specialise in different products
questions.why: Cultural diffusion is the spread of cultural elements from one group to another, and in pre-colonial Nigeria it travelled along the routes of war and of trade. The first option is the definition of inter-group relations itself. The third describes society. The fourth describes trade, which is a channel of diffusion but not what the term means.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the Portuguese role in the trans-Atlantic slave trade is correct?
options: They joined the Dutch as the leading traders in the 17th century
They were granted the Americas by the Pope, while Africa went to Spain
They were the first European power to run a regular slave trade from West Africa to the Americas
They were the biggest traders of the 18th century, carrying more than half of all slaves
questions.concept: Portuguese primacy in the slave trade
questions.why: The Portuguese were the first European power to establish a regular trade in slaves from West Africa to the Americas, and they developed the triangular route. It was the Dutch who joined the Portuguese in the 17th century, not the reverse. The Pope ceded Africa to Portugal and the Americas to Spain, so the second option reverses the grant. Carrying more than half of all slaves in the 18th century is the British record.

questions.q: Put these in the order in which they dominated the trans-Atlantic slave trade: (A) the British; (B) the Dutch alongside the Portuguese; (C) Europeans already settled in the New World; (D) the Portuguese.
questions.why: The Portuguese were the chief slave traders in West Africa before 1600, the Dutch joined them as leading traders in the 17th century, the British were the biggest in the 18th century, and in the 19th century Europeans who had settled in the New World organised much of what remained. That gives D, B, A, C. The other three orders promote either the British or the Dutch a century or more too early.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the four named implications of the slave trade for Africa?
options: Destruction of Africa's socio-economic and political structures
The introduction of a common currency across West Africa
questions.concept: Implications of the slave trade for Africa
questions.why: The four implications are depopulation, destruction of Africa's socio-economic and political structures, unbridled warfare, and insecurity leading to underdevelopment. A common currency is the outsider and the opposite of what happened: the trade fragmented economies and drove communities to relocate away from the slavers' routes.

questions.q: Which of the following pairs a scholar with the claim credited to him?
options: Phillip Curtin: over 7 million Africans died in transit
Washington Alcott: the trade removed millions, including many skilled tradesmen and women
Paul Lovejoy: the largest intercontinental migration in western history
Claude Ake: underdevelopment is the outcome of the twin evils of slavery and colonialism
questions.why: Washington Alcott is credited with the forced removal of millions, including a large percentage of skilled tradesmen and women. The 7 million who died in transit is Paul Lovejoy's figure and the largest intercontinental migration over 300 years is Phillip Curtin's phrase, so the first and third options exchange those two. The twin evils line is Wole Soyinka's, shared by Walter Rodney; Claude Ake blamed the stagnation of productive forces.

questions.q: How long did the Middle Passage take, and how many captives did a single ship carry?
questions.why: The crossing took 5 to 8 weeks in terrible conditions, and with each captive allotted a space of 6 ft by 1 ft by 4 inches a ship carried between 451 and 600 people. The first option shrinks weeks to days, which no crossing of that era could manage. The second and third keep the shape of the answer but alter both figures.

questions.q: An expedition of 1857 led to the establishment of three trading ports in the Delta. Which three?
questions.why: Macgregor Laird's expedition of 1857 produced the Delta ports of Ado, Onitsha and Gbebe, and Laird himself was granted admiralty in the Delta. Bonny, Brass, Opobo, Old Calabar, Forcados and Benin are districts of the Oil River Protectorate, which was not established until 1884. Lagos, Epe and Badagry belong to the annexation story rather than to the expedition.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the decline of the Royal Niger Company is correct?
options: Sir Ralph Moor was appointed Consul of the Oil River Protectorate in 1884
Salisbury's appointment as Colonial Secretary weakened the company
The Kirk Commission was set up to look into the raid on Akassa by the Brass people
The charter was revoked after the company won its price war
questions.concept: Decline of the Royal Niger Company
questions.why: The Kirk Commission of Enquiry was set up over the Akassa raid, and the revocation of the charter followed. Sir Ralph Moor became Consul of the Oil River Protectorate in 1891; 1884 is the year of Consul Hewett's treaty-making tour. Salisbury as Colonial Secretary shielded the company from its critics, and it was Joseph Chamberlain's appointment that helped weaken it. The price war was one of the causes of decline, not a victory.

questions.q: In the triangular trade, what role did each of the three corners play?
options: Africa the organiser, Europe the source, the Americas the destination
Africa the source, the Americas the destination, Europeans the organisers
Europe the source, Africa the destination, the Americas the organisers
The Americas the source, Africa the destination, Europeans the organisers
questions.why: Africa was the source of the captives, the Americas the destination where they worked the mines and the cotton, sugar and tobacco plantations, and Europeans were the organisers of the traffic. The sea leg between the first two corners is the Atlantic or Middle Passage. Each wrong option moves at least one corner, and Africa is never the organiser or the destination.

questions.q: What is meant by 'legitimate' trade in nineteenth-century West Africa?
options: Trade licensed by the Spanish crown in the New World
Trade across the Sahara in gold and salt
Trade with Europe in commodities such as palm oil and ivory rather than in people
Trade conducted by a company holding a royal charter
questions.why: Legitimate trade is trade with Europe in commodities such as palm oil and ivory instead of in human beings, and it expanded as the slave trade was closed down. Trade licensed by the Spanish crown in the New World is the Asiento. Gold and salt across the Sahara is the separate northern route. Trade under a royal charter describes the Royal Niger Company from 1886, a later arrangement rather than a definition.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the criticisms made of the Clifford Constitution of 1922?
options: Northern Nigeria was not represented in the council
It abolished the office of Lieutenant Governor
questions.why: The four criticisms are the Governor's veto power, the absence of local input in drafting, a predominantly white council, and the exclusion of Northern Nigeria, which laid a foundation for disintegration. Abolishing the office of Lieutenant Governor is the outsider: that was Sir Donald Cameron's work as Governor between 1930 and 1936, along with abolishing the provincial court and introducing the separation of powers.

questions.q: One constitution introduced regionalism and a later one introduced federalism. Which pairing is correct?
options: Clifford 1922 introduced regionalism; Richards 1947 introduced federalism
Richards 1947 introduced regionalism; Lyttleton 1954 introduced federalism
Macpherson 1951 introduced regionalism; Lyttleton 1954 introduced federalism
Richards 1947 introduced regionalism; Macpherson 1951 introduced federalism
questions.why: Richards in 1947 introduced regionalism, giving each of the three regions a House of Assembly while keeping one central legislative council. Lyttleton in 1954 introduced the federal system, sharing law-making power between centre and regions and creating the office of Premier. Clifford's innovation in 1922 was the elective principle, and Macpherson's in 1951 was wide consultation and the House of Representatives, so every other pairing misplaces one of the two.

questions.q: The Executive Council under the Macpherson Constitution was made up of a fixed list of officers. Which of the following was NOT one of them?
questions.why: The Council comprised three Chief Commissioners, one for each region, together with the Attorney General, the Financial Secretary, the Director of Medical Services and the Director of Education. The Director of Public Works is the plausible outsider: a real colonial office, but not one named on this body.

questions.q: One arrangement gave the Governor the title Prime Minister; another created the office of Premier in the regions. Which constitutions were they?
options: Prime Minister under Lyttleton 1954; Premier under Macpherson 1951
Prime Minister under Richards 1947; Premier under Lyttleton 1954
Prime Minister under Macpherson 1951; Premier under Lyttleton 1954
Prime Minister under Macpherson 1951; Premier under Richards 1947
questions.why: Macpherson's Council of Ministers in 1951 was constituted with the Governor as Prime Minister and twelve ministers, those ministers holding no ministries or portfolios. Lyttleton in 1954 created the position of Premier as leader of government in each region. The first option swaps the two, and the Richards Constitution created neither office.

questions.q: A party set out to unite the peoples of Northern Nigeria, retain northern regional autonomy and enhance the power of traditional Muslim rulers. Which party was it?
questions.why: Those three objectives belong to the Northern Peoples Congress, formed in 1951 out of the cultural body Jam'iyyar Mutanen Arewa with Ahmadu Bello, the Sardauna of Sokoto, as President. The Nigeria Youth Movement aimed at improving Yaba Higher College, independence and national unity. The Action Group aimed to forestall NCNC control of the Western Region. The NNDP was Macaulay's Lagos party of 1923.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the Nigeria Youth Movement is correct?
options: In 1938 it won all the elective seats from the NNDP
It published the West African Pilot
It was founded in 1923 by Herbert Macaulay
It was destroyed in 1951 by the formation of the Action Group
questions.why: The NYM took all the elective seats from the NNDP in 1938, having grown out of the Lagos Youth Movement once Azikiwe, Awolowo and Abayomi joined. The West African Pilot belonged to the NCNC; the NYM's paper was the Daily Service. The 1923 founding by Macaulay is the NNDP. The NYM was destroyed in 1944 by internal party disputes, the same year the NCNC was formed.

questions.q: Which pairing of a party with its newspaper is correct?
options: The NCNC and the Lagos Daily News
The NNDP and the West African Pilot
The Nigeria Youth Movement and the Daily Service
The Action Group and the Daily Times
questions.why: The Nigeria Youth Movement established the Daily Service. The Lagos Daily News belonged to the NNDP and the West African Pilot to the NCNC, so the first two options exchange those papers. No newspaper is credited to the Action Group, and the Daily Times is not among the party papers at all.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the Amalgamation of 1914 is correct?
options: It gave Nigeria its first written constitution
It was carried out by Sir Hugh Clifford
It created a council of 45 members, four of them elected
It united Northern and Southern Nigeria into a single nation
questions.why: The amalgamation joined Northern and Southern Nigeria into one country, bringing together diverse ethnic groups, cultures, languages and traditions. The first written constitution came eight years later under Clifford in 1922, and it was Clifford's council that had 45 members with four elected. Clifford took over only in 1919; what Lugard set up in 1914 was the Nigerian Council of 36 members with advisory functions only.

questions.q: What did the elective principle, introduced in 1922, mean in practice?
options: Some members of the legislative council were chosen by election
Power was shared between the centre and the regions
Each of the three regions was given its own House of Assembly
The Governor could veto any bill before the council
questions.why: The elective principle meant that some council seats were filled by election rather than by nomination, four of the 45 in all, three for Lagos and one for Calabar. Sharing power between centre and regions is federalism, from Lyttleton in 1954. Regional Houses of Assembly came with Richards in 1947. The Governor's veto is a criticism of the same constitution, not the meaning of its innovation.

questions.q: A Chief of Army Staff seized power from a regime he called rigid and uncompromising, in a bloodless takeover made easy because the Head of State was away from Lagos and his deputy was out of the country. Who took power, and from whom?
questions.why: Babangida was Chief of Army Staff when he removed Buhari in 1985, calling that regime rigid and uncompromising; the coup was bloodless because Buhari was not in Lagos and his vice president Idiagbon was abroad. Buhari's own coup of 1983 removed Shagari after his re-election. Abacha removed Shonekan on 17 November 1993. Gowon was removed in 1975 by plotters led by Colonel Joseph Nanven Garba, who then installed Murtala Muhammed.

questions.q: Between 1960 and 1966 agriculture's share of GNP moved one way while manufacturing and mining moved the other. Which figures belong to agriculture?
questions.why: Agriculture fell from 63.4% to 55.6% of GNP in those years, even while national income grew at about 5% a year. Manufacturing rose from 3.6% to 6.2% and mining from 0.9% to 4.8%, which are the first two options. The last option keeps agriculture's two figures but reverses the direction, turning a falling share into a rising one.

questions.q: Which of the following was NOT one of the crises that destabilised Nigeria's First Republic?
options: The annulment of the June 12 presidential election
The creation of the Mid-Western Region
questions.why: The crises listed run from the 1959 election, fear of dominance, the quota system and disproportionate project allocation through the Western Region crisis, the creation of the Mid-Western Region, the census crisis of 1962 to 1963, the 1964 election crisis between UPGA and NNA, and the Western Region election of 1965. The June 12 annulment is the outsider by almost thirty years: it happened under Babangida in 1993 and produced Shonekan's interim government.

questions.q: Which pairing of a writer with his work is correct?
options: Chinua Achebe and A Dance of the Forests, 1960
Wole Soyinka and Things Fall Apart, 1958
Uche Okeke and The Palm-Wine Drinkard, 1952
Amos Tutuola and The Palm-Wine Drinkard, 1952
questions.why: Amos Tutuola wrote The Palm-Wine Drinkard in 1952. Things Fall Apart of 1958 is Chinua Achebe's and A Dance of the Forests of 1960 is Wole Soyinka's, so the first two options exchange those authors. Uche Okeke was one of the sculptors who drew on the pre-colonial past and traditional design motifs, not a novelist.

questions.q: Which of the following was NOT one of the three reasons the federal government gave for refusing to let the East secede?
options: Belief in the practicability of Nigerian unity
The prospect of Biafra leaving with the oil-producing states
The risk of losing Nigeria's access to the sea
The fragmentation of Nigeria into small states
questions.why: The three reasons were belief in the practicability of Nigerian unity, the danger of fragmenting Nigeria into small states, and the prospect of Biafra leaving with the oil-producing states. Access to the sea is the outsider: Lagos and the western coast were never in question, and the federal side was able to blockade the coastline precisely because it held the sea.

questions.q: After secession was declared, the federal side created twelve states, blockaded the coastline and changed the currency. What was this meant to achieve, and what followed instead?
options: To starve the federal army of recruits; instead it prolonged the fighting
To force the OAU to mediate; instead the OAU refused to intervene
To bring Ojukwu back to the Aburi talks; instead he fled to Ivory Coast
To isolate the Igbos and provoke an internal uprising; instead it won international sympathy for Biafra
questions.why: Three of the twelve states were carved out of the East and only one was predominantly Igbo, and the blockade and currency change were meant to isolate the Igbos and strangle the Biafran economy into an internal uprising. What came instead was malnutrition and inflation that Biafran propaganda turned into international sympathy and support, which prolonged the war. The OAU treated the conflict as a war between two independent nations, and Ojukwu's flight came only at the collapse in 1970.

questions.q: How many easterners were massacred in the northern pogrom, and what did the killings immediately produce?
options: Up to 3 million, and the collapse of Biafra
Between 8,000 and 10,000, and the Aburi Accord
Between 80,000 and 100,000, and a mass return of Igbos to the East
Between 80,000 and 100,000, and the immediate declaration of Biafra
questions.why: Between 80,000 and 100,000 easterners were massacred in the north, which sparked revenge killings of northerners in the East and a mass return of Igbos to their region. Up to 3 million is the death toll of the whole war, with another 3 million displaced. The Aburi Accord was a later attempt at negotiation, and the declaration of Biafra came later still, on 30 May 1967, after those talks failed.

questions.q: What was the national question that emerged after independence?
options: Whether Nigeria should keep a federal or a unitary constitution
What is Nigeria, who are Nigerians, and how is a national identity to be developed
Which region should control the revenue from crude oil
Whether the regional development corporations should be kept
questions.why: The national question is what independence in 1960 left unanswered: what Nigeria is, who Nigerians are, and how a meaningful national identity is to be built. It was sharpened by a regional system in which national power had to be reached through regional power first, which bred the fear of domination. The other options name real arguments of the period, but each is a single policy dispute rather than the question of identity itself.

questions.q: Before independence agriculture accounted for over fifty per cent of one measure, and in 1960 for over 75% of another. Which pairing is correct?
options: Over 50% of GDP, and over 75% of the workforce
Over 50% of the workforce, and over 75% of GDP
Over 50% of exports, and over 75% of GDP
Over 50% of GDP, and over 75% of export earnings
questions.why: Agriculture accounted for over fifty per cent of GDP before independence and absorbed over 75% of the workforce in 1960. One figure is output and the other is employment, which is exactly what the second option swaps. The third and fourth move one of the two onto exports, a measure neither number describes.

questions.q: Nigeria had two oil booms that left it no better off, and for different reasons. Which pairing is correct?
options: The 1970s boom was looted into foreign banks; the 1990s boom went unsaved
The 1970s boom went unsaved; the 1990s boom was looted into foreign banks
Both booms were spent on the Structural Adjustment Programme
The 1970s boom funded the civil war; the 1990s boom funded austerity measures
questions.why: In the 1970s boom the government saved nothing for a rainy day, so when the oil market crunched there was nothing to fall back on and agriculture had already been abandoned. In the 1990s boom the Head of State, Sani Abacha, looted the treasury and kept the funds in foreign banks. The first option reverses the two failures. SAP was a response to the crunch rather than something a boom paid for, and the civil war ended in January 1970, before the boom took hold.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the Structural Adjustment Programme is correct?
options: It was adopted before the austerity measures of the Buhari regime
It strengthened the currency, which has risen steadily since
It destroyed the manufacturing base as the economy was flooded with imported goods
It was adopted without any pressure from outside Nigeria
questions.concept: Effects of the Structural Adjustment Programme
questions.why: SAP flooded the economy with imported goods against which local products could not compete on price or quality, and so destroyed the manufacturing base. Austerity measures came first, under the Buhari regime in the mid-1980s, and SAP followed under IMF pressure, which disposes of the first and last options. The currency began a downward movement under SAP and has continued down, not up.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the named causes of Nigeria's economic problems?
options: The crash of share prices and the economic meltdown
Over-dependence on crude oil for government revenue
Untimely implementation of the national budget
questions.why: The crash of share prices and the economic meltdown are the consequence of insider abuses, non-performing loans and round-tripping, not a cause in their own right. Over-dependence on crude oil, pipeline vandalisation and untimely implementation of the budget are all on the list of causes, alongside corruption and poor economic policies.

questions.q: Which of the following is one of the solutions offered for Nigeria's economic problems?
options: Devaluing the currency to boost exports
questions.why: Investing in tourism is one of the ten solutions, alongside economic diversification, curbing corruption, providing electricity for manufacturing, building industrial parks and clusters, boosting local refining capacity, improving the political-economic structure, reducing the cost of governance and effective tax collection. The other three are plausible policy moves that appear nowhere on that list, and devaluation runs against an account in which the currency has been falling since SAP.

questions.q: A Swiss-based consultant warned that Nigerian crude might have to be sold at a discount to reach new markets in Asia. What prompted the warning?
options: Shale oil production had left the United States awash with light crude
India had cut its purchases of Nigerian crude
Pipeline vandalisation had halved Nigerian output
The IMF had demanded that Nigeria sell its crude at a discount
questions.why: Olivier Jakob's warning followed United States shale production: with the country awash with light crude it might one day need no Nigerian oil, and in 2014 the United States, then the largest buyer, announced reduced purchases. India then replaced it as the major buyer, so India bought more rather than less. Vandalisation is a separate cause of economic trouble, and what the IMF pressed for was the adoption of SAP.

questions.q: Colonial intrusion transformed Nigeria's precolonial economy into which model?
questions.concept: Colonial transformation of the indigenous economy
questions.why: Colonial intrusion replaced the indigenous system with the Western capitalist economic model, reorienting production towards export cash crops and displacing local crafts with imported manufactures, and altering social and political structures with it. Nothing centrally planned or socialist was imposed. Exchange did not end, it was redirected towards Europe. The trans-Saharan network long predated colonial rule and was not what colonialism created.

questions.q: Why did exchange become necessary in Nigeria's indigenous trade system between 1500 and 1800 AD?
options: A common currency had been adopted across the regions
Geography and natural resources made regions specialise, so no community was self-sufficient
Colonial officials required communities to trade with one another
The apprenticeship system obliged every craftsman to sell outside his own town
questions.concept: Why the indigenous trade system arose
questions.why: Soil, rainfall, vegetation and mineral endowment made regions unequal in what they could produce, so communities specialised in agriculture, trade or craftsmanship and traded what they had for what they lacked. The Niger River carried the goods and international markets drew traders from further afield. No common currency is claimed for the period, colonial rule came centuries later and broke the system rather than starting it, and the apprenticeship system passed on skills rather than compelling sales.

questions.q: A suspect dies in a police cell after officers beat him and then leave him without attention. Which of the four named categories of extra-judicial killing does this fall under?
options: Law enforcement officials acting in the street
questions.why: The four categories are law enforcement officials, non-state actors, death sentences, and deaths in custody due to use of force or failure to protect the right to life. A man who dies in a cell after force and neglect is a death in custody. Death sentences are judicial executions; non-state actors are killers outside the security forces; the street-arrest option describes killings by officials outside custody, which is the neighbouring category.

questions.q: A State fixes 18 as the minimum age of marriage for both boys and girls and enforces it, yet a local government chairman personally officiates at the wedding of a 14-year-old girl. Which part of the five-part test does the State fail?
options: It has not established a minimum age of marriage
It involves public officials in child marriage
It has set different ages for boys and girls
It has failed to enforce the minimum age
questions.why: A State violates international human rights law if it fails to establish a minimum age, fails to enforce it, sets different ages for boys and girls, fails to act with due diligence to prevent child marriage, or involves public officials in it. Here the age is set, the same for both sexes and enforced, so the failing limb is the involvement of a public official, the chairman. The other three options describe limbs the stem says the State has satisfied.

questions.q: Put these four events in the order they happened: (A) the Violence Against Persons (Prohibition) Act is signed into law; (B) a Constitution introduces the Fundamental Objectives and Directive Principles of State Policy; (C) the #EndSARS protests bring international attention to police brutality; (D) a Constitution places human rights in Chapter IV, Sections 33 to 46.
questions.concept: Timeline of Nigerian human rights instruments
questions.why: The 1979 Constitution introduced the Fundamental Objectives and Directive Principles (B), the 1999 Constitution holds Chapter IV (D), the VAPP Act was signed in 2015 (A) and #EndSARS was October 2020 (C), so the order is B, D, A, C. 'B, A, D, C' dates the VAPP Act before 1999; 'D, B, A, C' swaps the 1979 and 1999 constitutions; 'B, D, C, A' puts the 2015 Act after the 2020 protests.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the three key principles of the rule of law?
options: Protection of individual rights through the courts
questions.concept: Principles of the rule of law
questions.why: The rule of law means a nation is governed by laws rather than the arbitrary decisions of officials, and its three key principles are supremacy of law, equality before the law, and protection of individual rights through the courts. Separation of powers is a real constitutional idea, and a plausible outsider, but it is not one of the three principles listed.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the National Human Rights Commission's caseload is correct?
options: It received 1,701,519 cases in 2021, up from 1,287,280 complaints in 2020
It received 1,287,280 cases in 2021, down from 1,701,519 in 2020
It received about 367,000 cases of rights violations in 2021
It handed 1,701,519 complaints to the National Broadcasting Commission in 2021
questions.why: The NHRC received 1,701,519 cases of rights violations in 2021, higher than the 1,287,280 complaints received in 2020, so the caseload rose. The second option swaps the years and reverses the direction of change; 367,000 is the figure for women and gender-related issues in 2021, not the NHRC caseload; the NBC regulates broadcast media and receives no such complaints.

questions.q: A lawyer wants to enforce her client's right to freedom of movement in a Nigerian court. Apart from Chapter IV of the 1999 Constitution, which instrument guarantees that such rights are enforceable in Nigerian courts of law?
options: Article 1 of the UN Declaration of Human Rights
The African Charter on Human and People's Rights
questions.concept: Legal framework for human rights in Nigeria
questions.why: The African Charter on Human and People's Rights is the instrument credited with guaranteeing that human rights are enforceable in Nigerian courts of law. The 2009 Rules are enforcement rules that still have shortcomings; the VAPP Act of 2015 deals with domestic violence and other abuse; Article 1 of the UN Declaration supplies the definition of human rights but is not what makes them enforceable in Nigeria.

questions.q: In Nigeria 43% of girls are married before their 18th birthday and 16% before the age of 15. What percentage of girls are married between their 15th and 18th birthdays?
questions.why: Girls married before 15 are also married before 18, so the share married between 15 and 18 is 43% minus 16%, which is 27%. 59% comes from adding the two figures instead of subtracting; 16% and 43% are the two published figures read off without doing the subtraction.

questions.q: Article 1 of the UN Declaration of Human Rights says that all human beings are endowed with which two things?
questions.why: Article 1 reads: all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights; they are endowed with reason and conscience and should act towards one another in the spirit of brotherhood. 'Endowed with' goes with reason and conscience. Dignity and rights is what people are born equal in, brotherhood is the spirit in which they should act, and life and freedom are not in the article at all.

questions.q: A Beninese man married to a Nigerian woman has lived and worked in Lagos for many years and wants to become a Nigerian citizen. Which route is open to him?
options: By registration, as the spouse of a Nigerian
By naturalisation under Section 27 of the 1999 Constitution
By registration under the Seventh Schedule
questions.why: Registration is open to exactly two classes: a non-Nigerian woman married to a Nigerian, and a person of full age born outside Nigeria with a Nigerian grandparent. A foreign husband is in neither class, so his route is naturalisation, the general route for a foreigner who has lived a long time in Nigeria, governed by Section 27. Citizenship by birth depends on parents or grandparents, never a spouse; the Seventh Schedule contains only the Oath of Allegiance.

questions.q: A man became a Nigerian citizen by naturalisation in 2010. In 2019 he is convicted and sentenced to four years' imprisonment. May the President deprive him of his citizenship on the ground of this sentence?
options: No, the sentence came more than seven years after he became a citizen
Yes, because the sentence is not less than three years
Yes, any naturalised citizen who is imprisoned may be deprived
No, only citizens by registration may be deprived
questions.why: The President may deprive a person who is not a Nigerian by birth if he is sentenced to not less than 3 years' imprisonment within 7 years of becoming a citizen by naturalisation. Here the sentence is long enough but 2019 minus 2010 is nine years, outside the seven-year window, so this ground does not apply. The second option checks the 3-year limb and forgets the 7-year limb; the third ignores both numbers; the fourth is backwards, since deprivation reaches citizens by naturalisation and by registration but never by birth.

questions.q: While Nigeria is involved in a war, a citizen of full age makes the prescribed declaration renouncing his Nigerian citizenship to take up another country's. What may the President do?
options: Deprive him of citizenship for disloyalty by act
Register it, since renunciation is the citizen's own act
Refer the declaration to the courts under Chapter IV
questions.why: A citizen of full age has the right to renounce his citizenship by the prescribed declaration, but the President may refuse to register that declaration where it was made when Nigeria is involved in a war, or where it is contrary to public policy. Renunciation is not deprivation, so the disloyalty grounds do not arise; registering it ignores the war exception; Chapter IV deals with fundamental rights, not renunciation.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the three things an applicant for citizenship by registration must prove to the President?
options: Residence in Nigeria for a long period
A clear intention to be domiciled or reside in Nigeria
That the prescribed Oath of Allegiance in the Seventh Schedule has been taken
questions.why: The applicant for registration must prove good character, a clear intention to be domiciled or reside in Nigeria, and that he or she has taken the prescribed Oath of Allegiance in the Seventh Schedule to the 1999 Constitution. Long residence in Nigeria is the mark of the naturalisation route under Section 27, not a registration condition.

questions.q: Put these instruments on Nigerian citizenship in the order they were made: (A) the 1999 Constitution, whose Chapter Three provides for citizenship; (B) the Nigeria Citizenship Act 1960; (C) the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria 1979; (D) the Nigerian Citizenship Act 1961.
questions.why: By year the order is the 1960 Act (B), the 1961 Act (D), the 1979 Constitution (C) and the 1999 Constitution (A): B, D, C, A. 'C, B, D, A' follows the order in which the three earlier instruments are commonly listed rather than their dates; 'B, C, D, A' puts 1979 before 1961; 'D, B, C, A' swaps the two Acts.

questions.q: A trader keeps two sets of books so that he can under-declare his income to the tax authority. Which duty of every citizen under Section 24 of the 1999 Constitution does he breach?
options: Make positive and useful contribution to the community where he resides
Render assistance to lawful agencies in the maintenance of law and order
Abide by the Constitution and respect legitimate authorities
Declare his income honestly and pay his tax promptly
questions.why: Section 24(F) makes it the duty of every citizen to declare his income honestly to appropriate and lawful agencies and pay his tax promptly, which is exactly what a false set of books defeats. The community contribution (D), assistance to agencies in maintaining law and order (E) and abiding by the Constitution (A) are separate Section 24 duties that the scenario does not turn on.

questions.q: Citizenship is often confused with another term that is of wider scope than citizenship. Which term?
questions.why: Citizenship is often confused with nationality, and nationality is of wider scope than citizenship. Naturalisation is one of the three routes to citizenship, not a wider term; domicile is what a registration applicant must intend; civic responsibility is the set of duties that comes with citizenship.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT sufficient, on its own, to make a person a Nigerian citizen by birth under the 1999 Constitution?
questions.why: A person is a Nigerian by birth if both parents are Nigerians, or either parent is a Nigerian, or any one of the grandparents is a Nigerian, so any one qualifying relative in that list is enough on its own. Marriage never founds citizenship by birth: a non-Nigerian woman married to a Nigerian applies by registration instead, and that is the route students slide into this list. The grandparent limb is the one most often doubted, but it is expressly there.

questions.q: Two of the six programmes listed under Operation Feed the Nation are dated 1978. Which two?
options: Agricultural Development Project and Agricultural Credit Guarantee Scheme
River Basin Development Programme and Rural Banking System
Green Revolution and Directorate for Food, Roads, and Rural Infrastructure
Agricultural Credit Guarantee Scheme and Rural Banking System
questions.concept: Programmes under Operation Feed the Nation
questions.why: The six programmes are ADP (1976), ACGS (1977), RBDA (1978), RBS (1978), GR (1980) and DFRRI (1986), so the two 1978 entries are the River Basin Development Programme and the Rural Banking System. ADP and ACGS are 1976 and 1977; GR and DFRRI are 1980 and 1986; ACGS with RBS mixes a 1977 entry with a 1978 one.

questions.q: A 1987 initiative set out to mobilise and empower Nigerians to participate in nation building, promote self-reliance, achieve social justice and drive economic recovery, on the recommendation of a Public Bureau. Which initiative, and who headed the Bureau?
options: The National Orientation Agency; Samuel Cookey
Operation Feed the Nation; Samuel Cookey
questions.why: MAMSER, the Mass Mobilisation for Self-reliance, Social Justice and Economic Recovery, was launched in 1987 following the recommendation of the Public Bureau headed by Samuel Cookey, with exactly that aim. The National Orientation Agency is the later body, created by Decree 100 of 1993, that absorbed MAMSER's functions, so pairing it with Cookey dates it six years too early. Operation Feed the Nation is the 1976 to 1980 agricultural initiative of General Olusegun Obasanjo, which is why his name and that programme are the tempting halves to mix in.

questions.q: To close a budget deficit a government raises income tax and at the same time cuts its own spending. Which of the three main types of austerity is this?
options: Revenue generation plus lower government spending
Higher taxes to fund government spending
Lower taxes plus lower government spending
questions.why: The three main types are higher taxes (revenue generation) to fund spending; revenue generation plus lower government spending; and lower taxes plus lower spending. Raising taxes and cutting spending together is the second type. The first type raises taxes without cutting spending; the third cuts taxes; fiscal consolidation is one of the six Nigerian examples of austerity, not one of the three types.

questions.q: A military government urges city dwellers to plant crops on undeveloped building plots so that the country can cut its dependence on food imports. Which programme is this, and whose government introduced it?
options: Operation Feed the Nation, General Buhari
Operation Feed the Nation, General Olusegun Obasanjo
questions.why: Operation Feed the Nation was an agricultural initiative of 1976-80 introduced by the military government of General Olusegun Obasanjo to address food security and reduce dependence on food imports, and its signature instruction was that urban dwellers should garden undeveloped building plots. Buhari's programme was the War Against Indiscipline, not OFN; WAI was about discipline, not farming; MAMSER was a 1987 mobilisation programme.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the four principles promoted by the War Against Indiscipline?
questions.why: WAI promoted punctuality, respect for queues, environmental cleanliness and adherence to traffic regulations. Patronising made-in-Nigeria products and services belongs to the National Orientation Agency's 'Change Begins With Me' programme, a plausible outsider from a different reorientation body.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the reasons Operation Feed the Nation fell short of its aims?
options: Seedlings, insecticides and tractors were not provided as promised
Farmers were sceptical of the new methods
The manpower needed to expand farming operations did not materialise
The WAI Brigade was high-handed with farmers
questions.why: OFN fell short because resources such as seedlings, insecticides and tractors were not provided as promised, activities were not effectively performed, farmers were sceptical of new methods and administrative officials did not do their job, and the manpower to expand farming did not materialise. The high-handedness of the WAI Brigade is the criticism of the War Against Indiscipline, a different programme under a different government.

questions.q: Strict, frugal economic policies used by a government to manage public debt, typically during economic hardship or budget deficits, are called:
questions.why: Austerity measures are strict, frugal economic policies used by the government to manage public debt, typically undertaken during periods of economic hardship or budget deficits. Structural adjustment is Babangida's specific programme under which austerity was deepened; reorientation strategies are the wider family of programmes for reshaping attitudes; fiscal consolidation is one example of an austerity policy, not the definition.

questions.q: Bodies that pursue reorientation promote good change through five kinds of activity. Which of the following is NOT one of them?
questions.why: The five activities are public awareness campaigns, educational programmes, skill development, counselling and community outreach. Enforcement of discipline through penalties was one of the three methods of the War Against Indiscipline in particular, not one of the five general activities of reorientation bodies.

questions.q: After the civil war, which body was established to handle reconstruction and rehabilitation, focusing primarily on the Eastern States?
options: Directorate for Food, Roads, and Rural Infrastructure
questions.why: Under Gowon's 3 Rs policy of reconciliation, reconstruction and rehabilitation, the National Rehabilitation Commission was established to handle reconstruction and rehabilitation, primarily focusing on the Eastern States after Biafra's surrender in January 1970. The NOA dates from Decree 100 of 1993; the Directorate for Social Mobilisation is MAMSER of 1987; DFRRI is a 1986 rural infrastructure programme under OFN.

questions.q: Which of the following correctly pairs a Third Wave (1980-90) artist with the sound he or she introduced?
questions.concept: Four waves of Nigerian popular music
questions.why: The Third Wave introduced Waka, Yo Pop and Afro Juju: Salawa Abeni found fame with her Waka brand, Segun Adewale with Yo Pop and Shina Peters with Afro Juju, while Wasiu Ayinde Marshall carried Fuji forward. The first two options swap Adewale's and Peters's genres, and the last gives Marshall Abeni's genre instead of Fuji.

questions.q: In the 1980s two international record labels signed Nigerian Juju stars. Which statement is correct?
options: Island Records signed Sunny Ade and Virgin Records signed Ebenezer Obey
Island Records signed Ebenezer Obey and Virgin Records signed Sunny Ade
Island Records signed Fela and Virgin Records signed Sunny Ade
Virgin Records signed Shina Peters and Island Records signed Ebenezer Obey
questions.concept: Four waves of Nigerian popular music
questions.why: In the Third Wave Island Records signed Sunny Ade and Virgin Records signed Ebenezer Obey. The second option reverses the two labels; the third attaches Fela, the Second Wave Afrobeat name, to Island; the fourth brings in Shina Peters, who introduced Afro Juju but is not credited with either label deal.

questions.q: A genre that in Nigeria became popular as feel-good, upper-class music was, in the country it was borrowed from, music that addressed social problems. Which genre, and which country?
questions.why: Highlife had gained popularity in Nigeria as feel-good and upper-class music, whereas in Ghana, from where it was borrowed, it addressed social problems; the Nigerian Civil War particularly affected it. Afrobeat is Fela's Nigerian creation, not a borrowed genre; calypso is a Caribbean influence on the First Wave but is not the genre described; Highlife came from Ghana, not the Caribbean.

questions.q: Put these pairs of artists in the order of the waves of Nigerian popular music they belong to, earliest first: (A) Remedies and Plantashun Boiz; (B) I.K. Dairo and Haruna Ishola; (C) Segun Adewale and Shina Peters; (D) Sikiru Ayinde Barrister and Ayinla Kollington.
questions.concept: Four waves of Nigerian popular music
questions.why: Dairo and Ishola are First Wave (1950-67), Barrister and Kollington are Second Wave Fuji (1967-80), Adewale and Peters are Third Wave (1980-90) and Remedies and Plantashun Boiz are Fourth Wave (1992 onwards): B, D, C, A. 'B, C, D, A' puts Fuji after Yo Pop and Afro Juju; 'D, B, C, A' starts with the Fuji pioneers; 'B, D, A, C' puts the 1990s groups before the 1980s ones.

questions.q: A report identified 164 cases of extrajudicial killings between January and September 2021, one year after the #EndSARS crisis. Which body produced it?
questions.why: Global Rights recorded 164 cases of extrajudicial killings from January to September 2021. The Cable's figure is 91 deaths from police actions between March 2019 and February 2020, before the crisis; Amnesty International's is 52 unlawful killings and 62 cases of arbitrary arrest, ill treatment and torture in the south-east over four months from January 2021; the NHRC's figures are its own caseload of rights violations, not this report.

questions.q: The #EndSARS movement produced 10 million new registered voters. Around 76% of them were young people, and 40% of those young registrants were students. About how many of the new registrants were young students?
questions.why: Young registrants are 76% of 10 million, which is 7.6 million; students are 40% of those, 0.40 × 7.6 million = 3.04 million, about 3.0 million. 4.0 million applies the 40% to all 10 million instead of to the young registrants; 7.6 million stops after the first step; 3.6 million comes from subtracting 40% from 76% and applying 36% to 10 million.

questions.q: A scholar argues that the Special Anti-Robbery Squad was born in a moment of turmoil: the failing economy after the oil boom, the depreciating naira, the civil war, the Structural Adjustment Programme and poor leadership. Who?
questions.why: Abimbola Oyarinu posits that SARS began during a moment of turmoil, listing the falling and failing economy after the oil boom, the depreciating naira, the civil war, SAP and poor leadership. Moses Ochonu's argument is a different one, that the Nigerian Police have not been decolonised and that brute force was their primary operating philosophy; Cheryl Johnson-Odim is quoted on Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti; Aliogo is the 2023 source on child marriage.

questions.q: Scholars trace the origins of popular culture to the creation of which class, generated by the Industrial Revolution?
questions.why: Scholars trace the origins of popular culture to the creation of the middle class generated by the Industrial Revolution. The working class appears in the next step of the story, as the people who moved into cities and created their own culture and lifestyle; the governing classes are the owners of the 'official culture' that popular culture is contrasted with; urban youth are who popular music primarily attracts, not the origin of popular culture.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the October 2020 #EndSARS protest is correct?
options: It was the first time Nigerian youths had protested against police brutality
It lasted three days before the army fired on protesters
It spread nationwide but was not popular in the northern part of the country
It was organised mainly through Facebook
questions.why: The protest soon spread nationwide but was not popular in the northern part of the country. It was not the first youth protest against police brutality; what was new was harnessing social media. It lasted three weeks, not three days, and ended with the army shooting at protesters at the Lekki toll gate. Twitter, not Facebook, was the platform especially deployed, with e-flyers giving the time and place of protests.

questions.q: A 76-year-old activist known as the Lioness of Lisabi was thrown from a second-storey window when soldiers raided her son's Lagos home on 18 February 1977. On what date did she die of her injuries?
questions.why: Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti was injured in the 18 February 1977 raid on Fela's residence and died on 13 April 1978. '18 February 1978' keeps the raid's day and month with the wrong year; '13 April 1977' puts her death in the raid year; 1997 is the year her son Fela died, not her.

questions.q: Put these events in the order they happened: (A) Wole Soyinka is imprisoned for 22 months for speaking out against the civil war; (B) Chinua Achebe publishes Things Fall Apart; (C) Nwankwo Kanu wins Olympic gold for Nigeria; (D) Soyinka flees Nigeria after being charged with treason.
questions.concept: Timeline of the Makers of Nigeria
questions.why: Things Fall Apart was published in 1958 (B), Soyinka was imprisoned in 1967 (A), he fled in 1994 (D) and Kanu's Olympic gold was 1996 (C), so the order is B, A, D, C. 'B, A, C, D' puts the 1996 gold before the 1994 flight; 'A, B, D, C' puts the 1967 imprisonment before the 1958 novel; 'B, D, A, C' has Soyinka fleeing before he was imprisoned.

questions.q: One year saw both Wole Soyinka receive the Nobel Prize for Literature and the magazine editor Dele Giwa die in a parcel bombing. Which year?
questions.concept: Timeline of the Makers of Nigeria
questions.why: Soyinka received the Nobel Prize in 1986, the first African to do so, and Dele Giwa was killed by a parcel bomb in the same year, 1986, the case Gani Fawehinmi later fought to reopen. 1983 is when Achebe became PRP deputy national vice president; 1994 is when Soyinka fled Nigeria; 1977 is the raid on Fela's home.

questions.q: During the 1920s Herbert Macaulay protested British colonial policies on three issues. Which of the following is NOT one of them?
options: The 1914 amalgamation of North and South
questions.why: Macaulay, the father of Nigerian nationalism, protested British policies on water rates, land issues and the management of railway finances. The 1914 amalgamation is a real colonial event of the period, and a plausible outsider, but it is not one of the three issues credited to his 1920s protests.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about Obafemi Awolowo is correct?
options: He was the last governor-general of Nigeria from 1960 to 1963
He founded the NNDP in 1923, Nigeria's first political party
He was premier of the Western Region from 1960 to 1966
He led the Action Group and campaigned for the federal constitution realised in 1954
questions.why: Awolowo led the Action Group and was at the forefront of the campaign for a federal constitution, realised in the 1954 Lyttleton Constitution; he was the first premier of the Western Region from 1954 to 1960. The last governor-general of 1960-63 was Azikiwe; the NNDP of 1923 was Macaulay's; the premiership dates 1960-66 are wrong, since his term ran from 1954 to 1960.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the honours credited to Nwankwo Kanu?
questions.why: Kanu won Nigeria the 1996 Olympic gold, beating Brazil and Argentina on the way, and won the African Footballer award, the Premier League, the UEFA Champions League and the UEFA Cup. The FIFA World Cup is the obvious outsider: it is not among the honours credited to him.

questions.q: Which radical, revolutionary and multi-ethnic youth body, inspired by Nnamdi Azikiwe, championed the struggle against imperialism and the belief that Nigerians should manage their own affairs?
questions.why: Azikiwe inspired the Zikist movement, a radical, revolutionary and multi-ethnic youth body that championed the Nigerian struggle against imperialism. The Nigerian Youth Movement is the body Macaulay's NNDP joined to form the NCNC; the Action Group was Awolowo's party; the Pirates Confraternity was the social group Soyinka founded at Ibadan in the early 1950s.

questions.q: The Nigerian diaspora contributes significantly to national development. Through which channel does it do so primarily?
questions.why: The Nigerian diaspora contributes to national development primarily through remittances, which have become a key source of foreign exchange and a major contributor to GDP. Tourism, foreign direct investment and return migration are other channels a student might guess, but remittances are the channel identified.

questions.q: A teenager begins snatching phones after watching older boys on his street do it and get away with it, copying their methods exactly. Which theory of crime best explains this?
questions.why: Social Learning Theory holds that criminal behaviour is acquired by observing and imitating others, which is what the copying describes. Rational Choice Theory would have him weigh cost or risk against benefit; Strain Theory would point to social structures pressuring him; Labelling Theory is a theory of deviance about being tagged deviant, not of learning by imitation.

questions.q: A politician pays a gang to abduct his rival so as to break his opponent's political power and popularity. Which of the two named causes of kidnapping does this illustrate?
questions.why: Only two causes of kidnapping are named: unemployment, where frustrated graduates who have hunted for work for three or more years turn to the crime to survive, and the political factor, where politicians engage the services of kidnappers to deal with their political opponents and their political power, popularity and economic muscles. Paying a gang to seize a rival is the political factor. Unemployment is the other named cause but does not fit a funded operation; societal decadence is one of the reasons people join cult groups; proliferation of firearms is one of the six causes of armed robbery.

questions.q: Prison records give armed robbery cases as 11,858 in 2013 and 10,249 in 2014. By how many cases did the figure fall?
questions.why: 11,858 minus 10,249 is 1,609, so armed robbery cases fell by 1,609 between 2013 and 2014. 1,619 and 1,709 come from slips in the subtraction (mis-borrowing in the tens and hundreds columns); 22,107 is the sum of the two figures instead of their difference.

questions.q: A student who is not himself a member is caught recruiting new students into an unlawful society on campus. What jail term does the law stipulate for him?
questions.why: The law stipulates a jail term of 21 years for anyone found to be a member of a cult group or who solicits for members of an unlawful society, so recruiting attracts the same 21 years as membership. 3 years is the sentence for allowing cult meetings in your residence or a structure you own; 7 years is the citizenship deprivation window, not a cultism penalty; 45 is the number of secret cults said to operate in tertiary institutions.

questions.q: Put these in the order they happened: (A) prison records show armed robbery cases falling to 10,249; (B) the Pirates Confraternity is founded at the University of Ibadan; (C) reported kidnap cases reach 4,600; (D) 838 kidnap cases are reported in Nigeria.
questions.why: The Pirates Confraternity dates from the early 1950s (B), the 10,249 armed robbery figure is 2014 (A), the 838 kidnap cases are 2018 (D) and the 4,600 are 2022 (C): B, A, D, C. 'B, D, A, C' puts the 2018 kidnapping figure before the 2014 robbery figure; 'B, A, C, D' reverses the kidnapping figures, making cases fall instead of rise; 'A, B, D, C' puts a 2014 statistic before a 1950s founding.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the six causes of armed robbery?
questions.concept: Causes and effects of armed robbery
questions.why: The six causes of armed robbery are the socio-economic factor, corruption, weak law enforcement, drug abuse, proliferation of firearms and the societal factor. Erosion of trust is one of the five effects of armed robbery, not a cause, which is the usual cause-and-effect mix-up.

questions.q: Which theory of deviance judges deviant behaviour on two criteria: a person's adherence to cultural goals, and a person's belief in how to attain those goals?
questions.why: Social Strain Typology is the theory of deviance based on two criteria, a person's motivations or adherence to cultural goals and a person's belief in how to attain them. Structural Functionalism says deviance plays a constructive role; Strain Theory is the theory of crime that says social structures pressure people to offend; Labelling Theory says deviance follows from having a deviant label applied.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the reasons given for why people join cult groups?
options: Unemployment among graduates searching for jobs for three or more years
Protection from boys of rival cult groups
questions.why: The reasons for joining cults include hostile and uncaring parenting, failing or expelled students, rivalry over girls, protection from rival cult boys, protection from victimisation by lecturers, peer influence, militarisation of the Nigerian polity, erosion of educational standards and societal decadence. Graduate unemployment after three or more years of job-hunting is the major cause of kidnapping, a different vice.
